title: The fire, the place, the prayer
hookLine: each generation forgot more of the ritual, but telling the story was enough

cards: Your grandmother made a dish nobody can quite get right anymore. The recipe was in her hands, not on paper. Your mother remembers most of it.
You remember some. Your kids may remember only that there was a dish, that it mattered, and the story of the kitchen it came from. Is that a loss?
Or is something still carried? Today's Hasidic story is about that kind of forgetting, over four generations of teachers. It's short, and it's a story about stories.

teach.h: THE FIRE, THE PLACE, THE PRAYER.

teach.b: When the Baal Shem Tov saw trouble coming for his people, he would go to a certain place in the forest, light a fire, and say a special prayer, and the trouble would be turned away.
Years later, when trouble came again, his successor, the Maggid of Mezritch, went to the same place. He said: I don't know how to light the fire. But I can still say the prayer.
And it was enough. A generation later, Rabbi Moshe Leib of Sassov went to the forest. I can't light the fire.
I don't know the prayer. But I know the place. And it was enough.
Then it fell to Rabbi Israel of Ruzhin. He sat in his chair at home, his head in his hands, and said: I can't light the fire. I don't know the prayer.
I can't even find the place.
All I can do is tell the story. And that has to be enough. And it was.
Each generation lost something real, and the story doesn't pretend otherwise. The fire, the prayer, the place: gone, one by one. But the story still carries the thread.

The telling keeps a door open. Many people know this tale from the writer Elie Wiesel, who opened one of his novels with it, after enormous loss. And plainly: the sources are late and the versions differ.
That seems right for a story about how stories survive.

how: Telling stories of the rebbes is itself a Hasidic practice, especially at the meal ending Shabbat, and this tale is often told to explain why.

the eternal light that burns above every synagogue ark

games.q: you're Israel of Ruzhin. trouble is coming. you can't light the fire, don't know the prayer, can't find the place. what do you do?
o: give up. it's all been lost.
tell the story of the fire.
go looking for the forest anyway.
games.why: he sat in his chair and told the story, and the tale says that was enough.

practice: Hold a story you love, from your family, your faith, your childhood, or from these lessons; if you only remember part of it, hold that part. Who's in it, what happens, and why does it matter to you?
Picture telling it to someone, a child, a friend, a partner, so it goes one more generation.

wordCard.voice: The fire. The Baal Shem Tov's fire, then only the prayer, then only the place, then only the story. And the story was enough.

carryVoice: Your line: the story is enough. Tomorrow, a rebbe afraid of one question. Day two hundred ninety-seven, done.
